definition: Able to express ideas clearly, gracefully, and persuasively, especially in speech.
example: His eloquent thank-you note brought his grandmother to tears.
nuance: Articulate means speaking clearly; eloquent adds grace and a power to move or persuade the listener.
prompt: A student gives a speech at her graduation ceremony.
options: Speaking without notes, she gave an eloquent tribute to the teachers who had believed in her.
Her eloquent remarks wandered for forty minutes, repeating the same joke three times.
The eloquent valedictorian mumbled and lost her place so often that listeners gave up following.
Because the microphone was so eloquent, everyone in the back row could hear her.
reasons: A moving, well-phrased tribute delivered with skill is exactly what the word describes.
Rambling and repetition show wordiness, not skill with words; that is closer to loquacious.
Halting, confusing delivery is the reverse of graceful, persuasive expression.
Volume and sound equipment have nothing to do with expressing ideas well.

practice.prompt: A museum guide describes a painting to a tour group.
options: The painting's frame was eloquent, carved from solid oak and very heavy.
The guide's eloquent description made visitors see the loneliness in the painted figure's face.
The guide was so eloquent that she could only point at the painting and shrug.
The eloquent guide kept chatting about her weekend plans while the restless tour group waited to move on.
reasons: Weight and material describe sturdiness, not any ability to express meaning.
Words that help listeners feel and understand something new show real expressive power.
Being unable to put thoughts into words is the opposite of this quality.
Idle, off-topic chatter is mere talkativeness, not moving or persuasive speech.
